chunks: [The right of the ruler and the right of the ruled:]

Then, from His rights, He, the Glorified, created certain rights for certain people against others. He made them so as to equate with one another. Some of these rights produce other rights. Some rights are such that they do not accrue except with others.

The greatest of these rights that Allāh, the Glorified, has made obligatory is the right of the ruler over the ruled and the right of the ruled over the ruler. This is an obligation which Allāh, the Glorified, has placed on each other. He has made it the basis of their (mutual) affection, and an honour for their religion. Consequently, the ruled cannot prosper unless the rulers are sound, while the rulers cannot be sound unless the ruled are steadfast.
ai.seo_question: What are the mutual rights between the ruler and the ruled in Shia Islamic governance?
ai.summary: In the context of Imam Ali’s governance during the Rashidun era, this passage from Nahj al-Balagha articulates the theological basis of political reciprocity, where the ruler's authority is contingent upon the people's obedience and vice versa. This mutual obligation (haqq) serves as a structural mechanism for 'al-ulfah' (social cohesion) and 'izz al-din' (honor of religion), reflecting the Shia principle that legitimate leadership requires a symbiotic relationship between the leader's justice and the community's piety. The text underscores that neither the ruler nor the ruled can achieve spiritual or social perfection in isolation, establishing a framework for just governance rooted in divine ordinance.
